title: What Humanity Needs To Flourish In The Next Decade | NOEMA
gist: Weyl, Evans and White argue that AI alignment is only half the problem and coin 'reverse alignment' for the neglected other half — redesigning institutions, credentials, markets and governance so societies can absorb AI. They open with the U.S. government ordering Anthropic to cut off Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign nationals, which the company implemented for every customer within hours, then specify concrete infrastructure bets: personhood credentials and verifiable credentials, zero-knowledge 'meronymity', C2PA provenance, a real training-data royalty market priced off data-mixture decisions and scaling laws, cross-provider agent trust standards, and portable interoperable labor credentials.

themes.theme: Capability-institution gap and three failure modes

insights.claim: Last month the U.S. government ordered Anthropic to cut off access to its two most capable models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, for all foreign nationals including its own employees, and within hours the company disabled the systems for every customer.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that a single jurisdiction can suspend frontier model access globally within hours — a concentration risk any enterprise building on a US frontier lab must underwrite.
insights.quote: Within hours, the company disabled the systems for every customer.
insights.locator: Editor’s Note / opening

insights.claim: Dario Amodei's June 2026 essay 'Policy on the AI Exponential' warns that AI capabilities climb exponentially while policy and social institutions move at their accustomed pace, a mismatch he likens to seeking military aid from trees.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Frontier lab leadership publicly forecasting institutional failure to keep pace is itself a signal that abrupt, poorly-designed regulatory intervention is the likeliest policy path.
insights.quote: a mismatch he likens to seeking military aid from trees
insights.locator: That gap has become a source of alarm

insights.claim: The Anthropic Institute released internal data on models that have begun to help build their own successors, giving fresh weight to long-running speculation about recursive self-improvement.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence of models contributing to their own successors compresses expected capability timelines and raises the value of compute owned by whoever runs that loop.
insights.locator: The same week, the company’s research division

insights.claim: For every dollar spent making AI systems more capable, only a tiny fraction goes toward the institutional, educational, organizational and civic infrastructure needed to integrate those systems productively and safely.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Identifies a structurally underfunded category — absorption infrastructure — where philanthropic and public capital is likeliest to be directed next.
insights.quote: The imbalance manifests in the flow of capital.
insights.locator: The imbalance manifests in the flow of capital.

insights.claim: Alignment is a two-sided problem: even a perfectly aligned system will underdeliver on its potential or cause serious harm if deployed into democracies, economies and legal systems unprepared to receive it — the authors call the neglected side 'reverse alignment'.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Reframes AI deployment risk as institutional readiness rather than model behaviour, which changes where diligence and regulatory attention should focus.
insights.quote: We call that neglected other side “reverse alignment”
insights.locator: We call that neglected other side

insights.claim: General-purpose technologies create broad value only after heavy complementary investment in new processes, skills and organizational redesign — when those complements lag, work gets reorganized faster than people can retrain, bargain or move, producing productivity without prosperity.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Explains why measured productivity gains can coexist with stagnant labour outcomes — the political backlash channel that AI-exposed sectors should expect.
insights.locator: Productivity without prosperity.

insights.claim: Once the cost of producing text, images and code collapses, the scarce input becomes human bandwidth to validate outputs, establish provenance and ensure accountability — decisions grow easier to automate than to justify.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Verification, not generation, becomes the bottleneck and therefore the pricing power — the strongest argument for investing in audit, provenance and validation tooling.
insights.quote: once the cost of producing text, images and code collapses, the scarce input becomes the human bandwidth to validate outputs, establish provenance and ensure accountability
insights.locator: Execution without verification.

insights.claim: AI makes states and large organizations far more capable while simultaneously lowering monitoring costs and concentrating discretion, pushing bureaucracies toward centralized control unless contestability, appeal and civil-liberties safeguards advance in tandem.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: AI as a centralizing technology is a governance risk that cuts across jurisdictions — relevant to sovereign risk and to the political durability of AI deployment.
insights.locator: Capacity without constraint.

themes.theme: Precedents that worked and one that half-failed

insights.claim: India Stack delivered Aadhaar biometric identity for over 1.3 billion people, instant free payments via UPI, DigiLocker data portability and eSign, bringing hundreds of millions of unbanked people into financial services and letting government transfers reach recipients directly.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: The clearest working example of digital public infrastructure at national scale, and the template other states will copy for AI-era identity and payments.
insights.locator: 4. India Stack

insights.claim: India Stack is also a cautionary tale: centralized biometric identity is surveillance infrastructure whose risks depend on the administering state's democratic health, and Aadhaar authentication failures have denied food rations, pensions and welfare disproportionately to low-caste, tribal and migrant communities.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: The same architecture that produced record financial inclusion created new vectors of exclusion — a warning to price political governance, not just technical design, into digital-ID exposure.
insights.quote: The same system that achieved financial inclusion at extraordinary speed also created new vectors of exclusion and control
insights.locator: Yet India Stack is also a cautionary tale.

insights.claim: Taiwan's Pol.is maps opinion clusters and surfaces 'bridging statements' that win support across divided groups, and the same bridging logic now runs at platform scale: X's Community Notes, adopted in 2021 and since copied by Meta and TikTok, are trusted across the political spectrum and roughly halve resharing of the posts they annotate.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: A measurable, already-scaled intervention that cuts misinformation spread roughly in half — the design pattern platforms will keep adopting in place of centralized moderation.
insights.quote: X’s Community Notes, adopted in 2021 and since copied by Meta and TikTok, are trusted across the political spectrum and roughly halve resharing of the posts they annotate
insights.locator: The same bridging logic now runs at platform scale

insights.claim: As the cost of producing convincing fake documents, biometrics and synthetic personas approaches zero, identity verification systems face an escalating crisis of trust, requiring 'personhood credentials' — cryptographic tools letting individuals prove they are unique real humans without revealing who they are.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Names a category — privacy-preserving proof-of-humanity — that becomes mandatory infrastructure for platforms, banks and elections as synthetic identity costs collapse.
insights.locator: Identification Systems

insights.claim: The W3C has standardized a Decentralized Identifiers protocol enabling portable personal digital wallets across private providers, and it already underpins pilot programs for educational credentialing and healthcare verification under the EU's eIDAS 2.0 framework.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: The standards and regulatory scaffolding for digital identity wallets already exist in the EU, making this a deployment story rather than a research one.
insights.locator: Emerging technical standards make this increasingly feasible.

insights.claim: Proving personhood alone only unlocks the lowest-common-denominator entitlements of all humans, because most of identity is relational — only architectures supporting proof of diverse social connections, like the W3C's Verifiable Credentials standard, can support digital community life.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Points the identity market beyond binary human-or-bot checks toward relational credentialing — a bigger addressable surface than proof-of-humanity alone.
insights.locator: But personhood alone is insufficient

insights.claim: Because AI agents are situated in social relationships rather than defined biologically, relational credential frameworks could authenticate agents as well as humans — supporting agentic commerce — and could let someone gain system access by having two already-trusted friends vouch for them rather than by fingerprint.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Agent authentication is the gating dependency for agentic commerce at scale — whoever sets that standard captures a toll position on machine-to-machine transactions.
insights.locator: Unlike biometrics, which define humans biologically

insights.claim: AI gives everyone access to a personal 'Sherlock Holmes', turning scattered digital traces — browsing, location, metadata, CCTV — into detailed behavioral profiles at minimal cost, which makes the transparency-versus-anonymity binaries encoded in laws like GDPR archaic and unworkable.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Existing privacy law is becoming technically obsolete, which means a legislative rewrite cycle in Europe and elsewhere is a matter of when, not if.
insights.quote: AI allows everyone access to a personal “Sherlock Holmes,” making scattered digital traces (browsing, location, metadata, CCTV) into detailed behavioral profiles at minimal cost.
insights.locator: Privacy

insights.claim: Cryptography already enables 'meronymity' — selectively revealing parts of identity — via zero-knowledge proofs, secure multiparty computation and federated learning, and these are not theoretical: they underpin social-media age verification, anonymous cryptocurrency transactions and encrypted messaging like Signal, with the real barriers being social and legal rather than technical.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on privacy-tech adoption is legal recognition, so watch statutory reform rather than cryptographic breakthroughs as the catalyst for this market.
insights.locator: Modern cryptography enables far richer possibilities

insights.claim: Provenance mandates are already law in three major jurisdictions: the EU's AI Act requires conspicuous disclosure of plausibly realistic AI-generated content, California's AI Transparency Act requires watermarking detectable by free tools, and China's Deep Synthesis Provisions require explicit signed consent from anyone imitated.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Watermarking and disclosure are already compliance obligations across the EU, California and China, creating a near-term mandatory market for provenance tooling.
insights.locator: Legislation already mandates digital provenance

insights.claim: The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity's content credentials standard attaches cryptographically signed metadata recording how content was created and modified, and paired with imperceptible watermarking enables high-confidence authentication of whether content is AI or human — while tools like VeriTrail trace generative claims back to source materials to locate where errors were introduced.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
entities: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity
insights.so_what: Names the specific standard and tooling layer that provenance regulation will be implemented through — the adoption path to track for compliance vendors.
insights.locator: A recent industry standards effort

themes.theme: A real market for training data

insights.claim: AI companies face a coming data scarcity because the next rounds of training demand fresh, high-quality human-generated data and the easy supply has been exhausted, while content creators are left choosing between modest one-off licensing deals and copyright suits, neither of which reflects their actual contribution.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Data scarcity plus unresolved compensation is the central unpriced input cost in frontier AI economics — a source of both margin pressure and litigation risk.
insights.quote: AI companies face a coming scarcity. The next rounds of training will demand fresh, high-quality human-generated data, and the easy supply has been exhausted.
insights.locator: Data Value

insights.claim: The standard objection that valuing training data at scale is impossible does not survive scrutiny, because AI companies already generate the two required datasets every time they train a model: data mixture decisions reveal how different sources should be weighted, settling how to divide the pie, and scaling laws reveal how much additional data improves a model, settling the size of the pie.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: If data can be priced from artifacts labs already produce, the main defence against royalty regimes collapses — raising the odds of a mandated compensation system and a new cost line for model developers.
insights.quote: That objection does not survive scrutiny because AI companies already generate the two datasets required for pricing, and they produce them every time they train a model.
insights.locator: The standard objection to a real market in training data

insights.claim: Collective management organizations — the bodies that license works and pay royalties across the music industry — supply the template for routing training-data compensation to large numbers of rights holders without negotiating each transaction individually.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Music-industry royalty infrastructure is the most likely institutional form for AI data payments — an existing playbook and set of intermediaries to watch.
insights.locator: What remains is distribution

insights.claim: Data value spans the whole AI lifecycle rather than just pretraining, and markets for later stages such as model steering and retrieval are already emerging — evidenced by the success of providers like Scale AI, which pays data workers around the world to help align and ground models.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Post-training data services are a proven revenue category, and healthy markets at each stage reinforce each other — supporting the data-labour and evaluation vendor thesis.
insights.locator: The value of data spans the whole AI lifecycle

insights.claim: Today's AI agents are built to be unconditionally helpful, which makes them dangerously naive collaborators liable to be tricked by online hackers into divulging their principals' confidential data — usable cooperative systems instead need human-like trust building: small exchanges first, track records, reliability assessed from both personal experience and group reputation.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Agent-to-agent security and reputation systems are an unbuilt layer standing between current agents and real multi-party automation — a clear infrastructure gap.
insights.quote: today’s agents are built to be unconditionally helpful, making them dangerously naive partners
insights.locator: Agentic Collaboration

insights.claim: Without shared trust standards that work across AI model providers, agents will cooperate only within walled gardens, letting incumbent platforms capture most of the value.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Directly actionable: absent interoperable agent-trust standards, value accrues to incumbent platform owners rather than to challengers or to the open ecosystem.
insights.quote: Without shared standards, agents will cooperate only within walled gardens, letting incumbent platforms capture most of the value.
insights.locator: Crucially, these trust systems must work across AI model providers.

insights.claim: When the business model shifts so that communities pay platforms for coherence rather than advertisers paying for attention, platform incentives align with the social fabric they depend on — with Taiwan's vTaiwan process and Japan's political 'broad listening' movement as working proof points.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: A named alternative monetization model for social platforms — community subscriptions for cohesion instead of attention advertising — worth tracking as a structural threat to ad-based revenue.
insights.quote: When the business model shifts so that communities pay platforms for coherence rather than advertisers for attention, platform incentives align with the social fabric they depend on.
insights.locator: Alternative designs, however, could focus on

themes.theme: Law, democracy and the research system

insights.claim: AI dramatically lowers the cost of surveillance, investigation, regulatory drafting and enforcement, and those capabilities accrue disproportionately to the executive branch, which already commands the operational machinery of the administrative state — while cheap plausible legal filings threaten to overwhelm courts whose legitimacy depends on careful deliberation.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: AI is an asymmetric power transfer toward executives, which raises regulatory and enforcement risk for any business that relies on procedural friction for protection.
insights.locator: Law & Liberties

insights.claim: Many frictions AI dissolves — the effort required to build a case, the practical limits on simultaneous investigations — have functioned as critical elements of constitutional order by screening out meritless or retaliatory exercises of state power before they could scale, so removing them without countervailing checks shifts power to a unilateral executive.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Reframes bureaucratic inefficiency as an unpriced civil-liberties safeguard — automation of state functions carries a governance cost that efficiency arguments ignore.
insights.locator: Many of the frictions AI dissolves

insights.claim: Restoring balance requires permanent audit trails for AI-assisted government decisions, AI-assisted case screening under human supervision to manage exploding dockets, and publicly available legal models letting ordinary citizens contest state action at comparable speed and cost — plus legislatures rebuilding the analytical capacity lost when the U.S. Congress's Office of Technology Assessment was defunded in 1995.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Specifies the govtech procurement categories — audit trails, docket triage, public legal models — that follow if legislatures respond rather than cede ground to executives.
insights.locator: Restoring balance requires equivalent infrastructure

insights.claim: AI models now generate hypotheses, run simulations and draft manuscripts at a pace that renders traditional peer review functionally obsolete, burying important breakthroughs beneath an avalanche of incremental recombination and outright slop.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Scientific publishing's gatekeeping function is breaking, which threatens journal economics and creates demand for AI-native evaluation and filtering systems.
insights.quote: Models now generate hypotheses, run simulations and draft manuscripts at a pace that renders traditional peer review functionally obsolete
insights.locator: Research

insights.claim: Promising experiments in the 'decentralized science' movement allocate research funding by tracing dependency patterns among open-source software, alongside mechanisms like quadratic and 'deep' funding, keeping science relevant as papers and labs give way to the open-source infrastructure supporting AI-driven innovation.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Dependency-graph-based funding allocation is a live experiment in reallocating research capital — watch whether major funders adopt it as the metric for scientific value.
insights.locator: The most explicit version would use such metrics

insights.claim: The true bottleneck to massive productivity gains from AI is not model capability but transforming organizations to process massively increased creativity and agency — eliminating hierarchical bottlenecks so workers join cross-cutting 'flash teams' whose operational data continuously feeds institutional learning.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Firm-level organizational redesign, not model access, is the differentiator in who captures AI productivity gains — a management-quality screen for AI-exposed companies.
insights.quote: The true bottleneck to massive productivity gains from AI is transforming organizations to process massively increased creativity and agency.
insights.locator: Workplace

insights.claim: The organizations that define the frontier of collective performance will be those that redesign workflows around AI's flexibility — much as factories were redesigned around miniaturized electric motors — rather than merely speeding up existing individual workflows, the equivalent of replacing steam engines with cheaper electrical ones.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: The electrification analogy sets expectations for a long lag followed by winner-take-most outcomes among firms that restructure rather than retrofit.
insights.locator: The organizations that will define the frontier

insights.claim: College has always built its most important capacities — close reading, perspective-taking, structured argument — implicitly as byproducts of content delivery, and AI makes that bundling untenable, so educators must become explicit about which capacities matter and use AI as a stationary bike for the mind rather than the 'e-bike' of Sam Altman's metaphor.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Reframes the AI-in-education debate around deliberate difficulty rather than assistance — an explicit rejection of the frictionless-assistant product direction.
insights.quote: using AI as a stationary bike for the mind, not merely the “e-bike” of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s metaphor
insights.locator: Education

insights.claim: Assessment must split in two — verifying foundational skills by prohibiting electronic assistance, and separately testing students' ability to accomplish things with AI that were previously impossible — and scaling both will itself require AI.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Implies a bifurcated assessment market: secure proctored testing plus AI-augmented performance evaluation, both requiring new tooling.
insights.locator: Assessment faces a parallel reckoning.

insights.claim: Model developers possess high-resolution signals on how human work is actually being reshaped through real-time interaction, yet states, workforce boards and community colleges lack the data-sharing frameworks and analytical capacity to translate those signals into responsive training or portable credentials.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: An exploitable information asymmetry: whoever bridges model-usage telemetry to workforce systems sits on the most current labour-market data in existence.
insights.locator: Labor Transition

insights.claim: Legacy unemployment insurance and workforce agencies were built for mass layoffs at a single employer and are unequipped for the diffuse, continuous task reallocation AI produces, so the fix is a 21st-century spine for labor mobility: interoperable, standards-based digital credentials portable across state lines, readable by workforce boards and interpretable by employers without the shorthand of a degree name.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Identifies interoperable portable credentials as the concrete infrastructure bet for AI-era labour transitions — a public-procurement-driven market.
insights.locator: At the core of such a redesign

insights.claim: History is full of failed sociotechnical visions: just over a decade ago multisectoral coalitions assembled policymakers, technologists and urban planners around 'smart cities' and most struggled to deliver, because converging experts often discover they disagree on what problem they are solving, what counts as evidence, whose expertise matters and what success looks like.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: The base rate for grand cross-sector technology coalitions is poor — a discount to apply to AI-governance initiatives making similar structural promises.
insights.locator: History is full of promising sociotechnical visions that failed.

insights.claim: Practical alignment mechanisms already exist: cross-sector secondments embedding technologists in government and civil servants in research labs, as done through the U.S. Intergovernmental Personnel Act and more recently the UK AI Security Institute, and advance market commitments that guarantee demand for products that do not yet exist.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Advance market commitments are the mechanism most likely to create bankable demand for sociotechnical infrastructure — the funding structure to watch for procurement opportunities.
insights.locator: There are mechanisms to help align participants

insights.claim: The binding constraint on this agenda is rarely the absence of good ideas but the absence of institutional arrangements that let different actors contribute what only they can, plus the patient capital willing to sustain those arrangements over the long period before results compound.
insights.speaker: E. Glen Weyl, James Evans and Chris White
insights.so_what: Names patient capital and coordination structures as the scarce inputs — the constraint that determines whether any of these infrastructure markets actually materialize.
insights.quote: History suggests the binding constraint is rarely the absence of good ideas but the absence of institutional arrangements
insights.locator: Reverse alignment is not a single project

source_meta.author: E. GLEN WEYL, JAMES EVANS AND CHRIS WHITE
